name: Rectus Femoris Muscle Flap

classification.mathes_nahai: Type II (descending LCFA dominant + minor distal muscular branches)

dominant_pedicle.artery: Muscular branch of descending lateral circumflex femoral artery

minor_pedicles: Distal profunda / superficial femoral muscular twigs
vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Enters deep posterolateral surface ~8–10 cm inferior to ASIS.
vascular_variants: Often preserved if sartorius/gracilis is compromised in complex groin vascular graft salvage

motor: Femoral nerve branch to rectus femoris
nerves.donor_numbness_note: Anterior thigh sensory decrease; ~15–20% terminal knee extension weakness unless vastus medialis/lateralis are centralized.

dimensions.thickness_notes: Bulky, sturdy muscle ideal for wrapping infected femoral bypass grafts and obliterating deep groin cavities.

arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Gold standard salvage flap for exposed/infected femoral vascular grafts, groin, perineum, lower abdomen, and ischium.

indications: Infected or exposed femoral vascular bypass grafts / groin lymphocele
Deep groin / pelvic / lower abdominal wall wounds
Functional free muscle transfer for elbow flexion
contraindications: High-demand ambulatory athletes (prefer gracilis/ALT to spare knee extension)
advantages: Large well-vascularized muscle bulk superior to sartorius for groin graft salvage
Rapid supine harvest
Strong distal tendon anchors securely
disadvantages: 15–20% reduction in terminal knee extension torque

donor_site.closure: Centralize vastus medialis and vastus lateralis together to distal rectus tendon stump; primary closure.
donor_site.functional_loss: Noticeable mainly on stairs/running (~15–20% quadriceps loss); mitigated by vastus centralization.

preoperative_planning: Verify profunda femoris / LCFA patency on vascular CTA
Counsel ambulatory patients on mild knee extension deficit
technique.design: Anterior longitudinal thigh incision from 10 cm below ASIS to 6 cm above patella.
harvest_steps: 1. Expose rectus femoris bipennate belly and divide distal tendon 3–4 cm proximal to patella.
2. Elevate muscle distal-to-proximal off vastus intermedius.
3. Identify and protect LCFA pedicle entering deep lateral aspect ~8–10 cm below ASIS.
4. Centralize vastus medialis and lateralis to distal quadriceps stump, tunnel muscle into groin, and drain donor pocket.
pearls: Suturing vastus medialis and lateralis together into the distal quadriceps stump significantly reduces postoperative extensor lag.
pitfalls: Failing to verify profunda femoris patency in vascular groin patients can cause total flap loss.

references.book: Mathes SJ, Nahai F. Reconstructive Surgery: Principles, Anatomy, & Technique

name: Anteromedial Thigh (AMT) Perforator Flap

classification.perforator_type: Septocutaneous (rectus femoris / vastus medialis) or Musculocutaneous

dominant_pedicle.artery: Innominate / medial branch of descending LCFA (or direct rectus femoris / SFA perforator)
dominant_pedicle.artery_origin: Lateral circumflex femoral artery (most common) or superficial femoral artery

perforators.label: AMT Perforator
perforators.location: Medial to rectus femoris / sartorius border at mid-thigh
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Often inversely proportional in size to ALT perforators (immediate bailout via same medial incision)

vascular_anatomy.angiosome: Medial descending LCFA / superficial femoral angiosome
vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Can be conjoined with ALT as a huge twin/mega-flap on the LCFA trunk.
vascular_variants: Variable pedicle origin (descending LCFA ~50%, rectus femoris branch, or SFA); absent in ~15–20%

sensory: Anterior femoral cutaneous nerve (for sensate flap)

dimensions.thickness_notes: Thinner and more pliable than lateral thigh skin in many patients; concealed medial thigh scar.

arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Primary intraoperative salvage flap via same incision when ALT perforators are absent; free flap for H&N and extremity.

indications: Immediate intraoperative bailout when ALT flap lacks usable perforators
Conjoined ALT + AMT mega-flap for massive defects
Thin H&N or extremity resurfacing with concealed medial scar
advantages: Accessible through the exact same medial ALT exploratory incision
Often thinner than ALT with concealed donor scar
Can be combined with ALT on a single LCFA pedicle
disadvantages: Less consistent perforator anatomy than ALT

preoperative_planning: Always Doppler anteromedial thigh during ALT marking as routine backup
Confirm perforator via initial medial ALT incision
technique.design: When ALT perforators are absent, retract medial edge of initial ALT incision medially and center skin paddle over AMT perforator.
harvest_steps: 1. Explore medial side of initial ALT incision subfascially over rectus femoris and vastus medialis.
2. Identify septocutaneous/musculocutaneous AMT perforator between rectus femoris and vastus medialis/sartorius.
3. Trace retrograde to descending LCFA (or superficial femoral branch) protecting femoral nerve twigs.
4. Commit medial skin incision only after confirming pedicle caliber and length.
pearls: An inverse relationship exists between ALT and AMT perforator caliber—when ALT has no perforators, look medially for a large AMT perforator.
pitfalls: Committing both skin incisions before visualizing the variable AMT vascular origin.

references.book: Blondeel PN et al. Perforator Flaps: Anatomy, Technique, & Clinical Applications

name: Posterior Tibial Artery Perforator (PTAP) Propeller Flap

perforators.label: PTAP Clusters (4–7, 9–12, 14–18 cm proximal to medial malleolus)
perforators.location: 1–2 cm posterior to medial tibial border along intermuscular septum
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Largest reliable perforators cluster ~8–12 cm and ~16–20 cm above medial malleolus

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Venous congestion is the leading complication after 180° propeller rotation; skeletonize ≥2–3 cm of perforator free of all fascial strands to distribute torsion.
vascular_variants: Verify posterior tibial artery patency with CTA/Doppler in distal trauma

sensory: Saphenous nerve (preserve alongside greater saphenous vein)

dimensions.thickness_notes: Thin, like-with-like distal leg skin without sacrificing a main tibial artery or muscle.

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: Selected PTA perforator adjacent to defect (rotates up to 180° as propeller)
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Covers distal third medial tibia, medial malleolus, Achilles tendon, and anterior ankle without microsurgery.

indications: Small-to-medium distal-third tibial / medial malleolus / Achilles defects outside zone of injury
Like-for-like non-bulky ankle resurfacing avoiding free flap
contraindications: Severe trauma/degloving in zone of injury around perforator
Occluded posterior tibial artery or severe PVD
advantages: Spares main posterior tibial artery and all muscles
Excellent distal leg contour and color match
No microvascular anastomosis needed
disadvantages: Higher partial tip necrosis / venous congestion rate (~15–20%) than free flaps in traumatized legs
Proximal donor defect often needs STSG

donor_site.closure: Primary if ≤4–5 cm (never close tightly over pedicle); STSG if wider.

preoperative_planning: Confirm PTA patency and locate perforators posterior to medial tibial border with Doppler / CTA
Commit only to exploratory incision first until best perforator is visualized
technique.design: Propeller blades centered on chosen perforator: major blade length = distance from perforator to farthest defect edge + 1–2 cm.
harvest_steps: 1. Make single exploratory anterior incision and inspect PTA perforators in septum directly.
2. Select largest pulsatile perforator outside zone of injury and design propeller blades around it.
3. Skeletonize perforator cleanly for ≥2–3 cm, dividing ALL perivascular fascial strands so twist distributes evenly.
4. Test clockwise vs counterclockwise rotation (pick direction with least twist), confirm capillary refill, and avoid tight closure.
pearls: Test BOTH clockwise and counterclockwise rotation directions and pick the one causing less visual vessel torsion.
pitfalls: Closing the donor site tightly over the rotated perforator causes delayed venous occlusion.

references.book: Blondeel PN et al. Perforator Flaps: Anatomy, Technique, & Clinical Applications
references.chapter_or_section: Posterior Tibial Artery Perforator Propeller Flap

name: Distally Based Peroneus Brevis Muscle Flap

classification.mathes_nahai: Type II / IV (distal constant peroneal pivot 4–6 cm above lateral malleolus)

dominant_pedicle.artery: Distal constant perforating/muscular branch of peroneal artery (~4–6 cm proximal to tip of lateral malleolus)

minor_pedicles: Proximal peroneal and anterior tibial muscular branches (ligated sequentially proximal-to-distal)
vascular_anatomy.angiosome: Peroneal artery distal lateral leg angiosome
vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Preserve axial intramuscular vessels and stop distal dissection 6 cm above the tip of the lateral malleolus.
vascular_variants: Verify intact peroneal artery on CTA/Doppler before harvest

motor: Superficial peroneal nerve (preserve main trunk and branches to peroneus longus)
sensory: Superficial peroneal sensory branch (emerges distally — protect)
nerves.donor_numbness_note: Dorsolateral foot numbness if superficial peroneal nerve is injured.

dimensions.thickness_notes: Slender, contoured muscle (~3–4 × 10–14 cm) ideal for small lateral malleolus, lateral calcaneus, or distal fibular hardware wounds.

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: 6 cm proximal to tip of lateral malleolus (constant distal peroneal pedicle)
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Covers lateral malleolus, exposed distal fibular plates, lateral Achilles, and posterior/lateral calcaneus.

indications: Small exposed distal fibular hardware / lateral malleolus wounds (≤4 × 6 cm)
Lateral calcaneal or distal Achilles small defects
Alternative to free flap in comorbid patients
contraindications: Peroneus longus absence/paralysis (sacrificing brevis loses all ankle eversion)
Occluded peroneal artery or severe lateral trauma
advantages: Rapid, simple harvest with primary lateral leg closure
Preserves peroneus longus eversion
Thin contoured coverage over lateral malleolus (fits in shoe)
disadvantages: Distal tip necrosis if dissected distal to 6 cm above lateral malleolus

donor_site.closure: Primary linear closure along lateral leg.
donor_site.functional_loss: Negligible ankle eversion loss when peroneus longus is intact.

technique.patient_positioning: Supine with hip bump or lateral decubitus under tourniquet.
preoperative_planning: Verify peroneal artery patency and intact peroneus longus
Mark 6 cm proximal to lateral malleolus tip as absolute stop-point
technique.design: Longitudinal incision over fibula from mid-leg down toward lateral malleolus.
harvest_steps: 1. Open lateral compartment fascia protecting superficial peroneal nerve; retract peroneus longus posteriorly.
2. Confirm intact distal musculotendinous junction and divide proximal origin of peroneus brevis off fibula.
3. Dissect proximal-to-distal ligating upper segmental pedicles while stopping strictly 6 cm proximal to lateral malleolus tip.
4. Release tourniquet, verify brisk distal bleeding, rotate into lateral malleolus/Achilles defect, and apply meshed STSG.
pearls: Never dissect closer than 6 cm to the tip of the lateral malleolus—that preserves the constant distal peroneal pedicle.
pitfalls: Confusing peroneus longus (superficial, longer tendon) with peroneus brevis (deep, muscular distally).

references.book: Eren S et al. Plast Reconstr Surg (Distally Based Peroneus Brevis Flap)

name: Pudendal Thigh (Singapore) Flap

classification.cormack_lamberty: Type A axial fasciocutaneous (posterior labial/scrotal artery)

tissue_components: Thin pliable medial thigh crease skin

dominant_pedicle.artery: Posterior labial (or scrotal) branches of internal pudendal artery

minor_pedicles: Obturator & medial circumflex femoral linking branches anteriorly

perforators.label: Internal Pudendal Perineal Perforators
perforators.location: Posterior to introitus/perineal body, medial to ischial tuberosity
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Emerge around posterior margin of labia majora / scrotal base

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Preserving deep epimysial fascia over gracilis/adductor origin protects axial subfascial blood supply.
vascular_variants: Rich anastomotic network around perineal body permits bilateral flaps for total neovagina

sensory: Posterior labial/scrotal branches of pudendal nerve + perineal branch of PFCN
nerves.donor_numbness_note: Preserves erogenous/tactile perineal sensation; scar hidden in crural fold.

dimensions.thickness_notes: Thin, pliable, sensate skin ideally suited for vaginal, vulvar, and perineal resurfacing without bulky muscle.

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: Posterior base lateral to perineal body / posterior introitus
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Reaches vulva, vaginal wall (unilateral or bilateral tubularized neovagina), perineum, and scrotum.

indications: Vulvectomy and partial/total vaginal reconstruction (bilateral Singapore flaps)
Perineal / rectovaginal fistula resurfacing
Scrotal reconstruction
contraindications: Severe pelvic radiation destroying internal pudendal vasculature
Massive deep pelvic exenteration dead space (prefer VRAM or gracilis)
advantages: Sensate, thin, pliable tissue matching vulvovaginal anatomy
Concealed donor scar in groin-thigh crease
No abdominal or muscle morbidity
disadvantages: Distal anterior tip necrosis if extended too far into femoral triangle
Hair-bearing skin may require epilation for vaginal canal
Insufficient bulk for large pelvic dead space

donor_site.closure: Primary tension-free closure hidden in groin-thigh crease.
morbidity: Wound dehiscence in moist groin fold

preoperative_planning: Map internal pudendal perforators medial to ischial tuberosity with Doppler
Keep width ≤6 cm for primary closure
technique.design: Posteriorly based 5–6 × 12–15 cm fasciocutaneous peninsula centered in the groin-thigh crease.
harvest_steps: 1. Incise anterior tip and lateral margins down through deep epimysial fascia over adductor longus and gracilis.
2. Elevate subfascially anterior-to-posterior, tacking fascia to dermis to avoid shear.
3. Stop posterior dissection at level of posterior introitus / perineal body to preserve internal pudendal perforators.
4. Tunnel beneath labia majora into vulvovaginal defect (or tube bilaterally) and close groin crease primarily.
pearls: Elevate strictly subfascially and preserve the posterior base at the level of the perineal body to safeguard internal pudendal branches.
pitfalls: Dissecting too aggressively posteriorly divides the entering internal pudendal perforators.

references.book: Wee JT, Joseph VT. Plast Reconstr Surg (Singapore Pudendal Thigh Flap)

name: Martius Labial Fat Pad Flap

classification.cormack_lamberty: Axial labial fat pad flap (dual posterior/anterior supply)

tissue_components: Vascularized fibrofatty labial pad (modified Martius omits bulbocavernosus muscle)

dominant_pedicle.artery: Posterior labial branch of internal pudendal artery (posteriorly based) OR external pudendal artery (anteriorly based)

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Dual anterior and posterior blood supply allows basing anteriorly for urethral/vesicovaginal or posteriorly for rectovaginal fistulae.
vascular_variants: Modern modified Martius uses the fibrofatty pad alone without harvesting bulbocavernosus muscle, minimizing bleeding

nerves.donor_numbness_note: Mild labial numbness or contour asymmetry.

dimensions.thickness_notes: Well-vascularized, pliable interposition pad (~2–3 × 7–9 cm) separating opposing urinary/vaginal/rectal suture lines.

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: Posterior labia majora (rectovaginal) or anterior mons/labia (vesicovaginal/urethral)
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Interposes directly between bladder/urethra and vagina, or between rectum and vagina.

indications: Complex vesicovaginal and urethrovaginal fistula interposition
Low-to-mid rectovaginal fistula reinforcement
Urethral diverticulectomy / sling erosion buttressing
contraindications: Severe labial radiation fibrosis or prior radical vulvectomy
High rectovaginal or massive pelvic exenteration defects (use gracilis or VRAM)
advantages: Rapid harvest (<30 min) with minimal morbidity
Dual anterior/posterior vascularity adapts to urinary or rectal fistulae
Significantly reduces fistula recurrence rates
disadvantages: Modest bulk (cannot fill large pelvic cavities)
Potential labial hematoma or minor asymmetry

donor_site.closure: Primary layered closure of vertical labial incision over small drain.

preoperative_planning: Choose posterior base for rectovaginal/mid-vaginal fistulae or anterior base for urethral/bladder-neck fistulae
technique.design: Vertical incision over hair-bearing labia majora harvesting fibrofatty pad deep to dermis.
harvest_steps: 1. Complete tension-free layered closure of primary urinary or rectal fistula first.
2. Make vertical incision over labia majora and mobilize fibrofatty pad preserving chosen posterior or anterior pedicle.
3. Create wide submucosal vaginal tunnel (2 fingerbreadths) to avoid pedicle compression.
4. Pass fat pad cleanly over repair line, tack with absorbable sutures, close vaginal mucosa, and drain donor pocket.
pearls: A wide (two-fingerbreadth) submucosal vaginal tunnel prevents venous strangulation of the fat pad.
pitfalls: Dissecting too deeply into bulbocavernosus muscle causes brisk venous bleeding without added clinical benefit.

references.book: Zenn MR, Jones G. Reconstructive Surgery: Anatomy, Technique, and Clinical Applications

name: Keystone Design Perforator Island Flap (Behan Types I–IV)

classification.cormack_lamberty: Multi-perforator fascial-lined trapezoidal advancement island (Behan Types I, IIA, IIB, III, IV)
classification.perforator_type: Randomly captured local musculocutaneous / fasciocutaneous perforators

tissue_components: Underlying perforator bed (no deep undermining except Type IV)

dominant_pedicle.artery: Multiple direct underlying musculocutaneous / fasciocutaneous perforators captured within central island base

perforators.label: Captured Deep Perforator Pedicle Bed
perforators.location: Beneath central body of trapezoidal keystone island
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Preserved completely intact without undermining in Behan Types I–III

vascular_anatomy.angiosome: Local regional perforasome (sympathectomy-like hyperemic 'red dot' phenomenon)
vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Preserving intact subcutaneous/perforator attachment underneath the island produces reliable robust perfusion.
vascular_variants: Do NOT individually skeletonize perforators — preserve entire central subcutaneous perforator bed

sensory: Local cutaneous nerves (preserves protective sensation in central island)
nerves.donor_numbness_note: Minimal compared to skin grafting; transient mild hyperemia.

dimensions.thickness_notes: Exact like-for-like local tissue match designed at a 1:1 flap-width-to-defect-width ratio with 90° lateral limbs (dual V-Y closure at ends).

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: Linear advancement perpendicular to long axis (recruiting laxity via dual V-Y at ends)
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Closes elliptical melanoma/trauma defects across trunk, thigh, lower leg, forearm, and face without skin grafting.

indications: Wide local excision (melanoma/sarcoma) defects on trunk, back, thigh, leg, and arm
Small-to-moderate lower leg / forearm defects avoiding STSG or free flap
Behan Type III double opposing keystones for large midline/limb defects
contraindications: Heavily irradiated or traumatized skin immediately adjacent to defect
Extreme tension zones (distal shin/ankle with zero adjacent laxity)
advantages: No perforator skeletonization or microsurgery required
Like-for-like color, contour, and sensation
Dual V-Y end closures redistribute transverse tension longitudinally
disadvantages: Wound edge tension/dehiscence if misapplied to tight distal extremity skin

donor_site.closure: Primary V-Y closure at both ends + direct advancement (Type I/IIA); STSG on secondary defect if needed (Type IIB).
morbidity: Longer surgical scar than simple graft
Minor edge epidermolysis under high tension

preoperative_planning: Orient elliptical defect parallel to cutaneous nerves/veins and longitudinal limb axis
Select Behan Type I, IIA (fascial division), IIB (STSG), III (double keystone), or IV (up to 50% subfascial undermining)
technique.design: Draw trapezoidal keystone island adjacent to defect on side of greater laxity: flap width = 1:1 defect width (W), lateral limbs drawn at 90° curving to outer arc.
harvest_steps: 1. Convert circular defect into an ellipse parallel to longitudinal neurovascular/dermatomal axis.
2. Mark 90° lateral limbs to width = 1× defect width and connect with outer curvilinear arc.
3. Incise full-thickness dermis and fat down to deep fascia WITHOUT undermining central perforator bed (divide outer deep fascia in Type IIA if needed).
4. Advance island using progressive V-Y closure at BOTH ends first to unload central tension, then close center.
pearls: Always close the two V-Y limbs at the ends FIRST—this converts longitudinal skin laxity into transverse advancement and dramatically reduces central tension.
pitfalls: Undermining beneath the central island divides the vertical perforators that keep the keystone alive.

references.book: Behan FC. ANZ J Surg (The Keystone Design Perforator Island Flap)

name: Bilobed (Zitelli) & Rhomboid (Limberg / Dufourmentel) Flaps
region: Local / Random Pattern (nose, cheek, temple, trunk)
tissue_components: Subcutaneous fat (or deep muscular-aponeurotic on nasal dorsum for bilobed)

dominant_pedicle.artery: Random subdermal & dermal-subcutaneous plexus (deep nasalis plane in Zitelli nasal bilobed)

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Limiting Zitelli bilobed total arc to 90° (45° + 45°) prevents standing-cone dog-ears and pincushioning.
vascular_variants: On the nose, elevate bilobed flaps in the deep plane beneath nasalis muscle above perichondrium/periosteum

dimensions.thickness_notes: Gold-standard geometric transposition flaps: Zitelli bilobed excels for distal nasal defects ≤1.5 cm; Limberg (60°/120°) and Dufourmentel rhomboids excel on cheek, temple, and trunk.

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: Zitelli bilobed: 90° total arc (45° + 45°); Limberg rhomboid: 60°/120° transposition aligned with RSTL
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Transfers adjacent skin laxity while controlling closing tension vectors away from free anatomical margins.

indications: Distal third nasal / tip / alar defects ≤1.5 cm (Zitelli bilobed)
Cheek, temple, periorbital, and trunk cutaneous defects (Limberg / Dufourmentel rhomboid)
Avoiding distortion of free margins (alar rim, lower lid, oral commissure)
contraindications: Defects >1.5–2.0 cm on distal nose (bilobed causes alar retraction — use paramedian forehead flap)
Active heavy smoking without deep-plane elevation
advantages: Precise mathematical control over closing tension vectors (keep secondary closure parallel to RSTL / LME)
Single-stage exact local skin color and sebaceous texture match
4 possible Limberg transposition options per rhomboid defect
disadvantages: Trapdoor / pincushioning deformity if inadequately undermined (bilobed)
Geometric zig-zag scars cross subunits if poorly oriented

donor_site.closure: Primary closure of secondary defect oriented perpendicular to LME / parallel to RSTL.
morbidity: Alar rim notching if primary lobe undersized

preoperative_planning: Identify Lines of Maximal Extensibility (LME, perpendicular to RSTL) by pinch test
Zitelli Bilobed: Primary lobe = 1.0× defect diameter (45°), Secondary lobe = 0.75–0.85× (90°), Burrow cone = 1× radius
Limberg Rhomboid: 60°/120° angles; short diagonal equals side length; orient donor closure parallel to RSTL
landmarks: Free anatomical margins (alar rim, lower lid)
technique.design: Test all 4 possible rhomboid flaps (2 off each 120° obtuse corner) and choose the one placing final donor tension parallel to LME.
harvest_steps: 1. Mark defect and pinch surrounding skin to determine optimal LME direction.
2. For Zitelli bilobed: draw 45° primary lobe (100% diameter), 90° secondary lobe (~80% diameter), and Burrow cone at pivot; elevate deep under nasalis on nose.
3. For Limberg rhomboid: draw 60°/120° rhombus with extension off 120° short diagonal and parallel 60° back-cut; for Dufourmentel bisect angle between short diagonal and side extension.
4. Undermine periphery broadly to prevent trapdooring, close secondary defect FIRST, then inset transposed lobes without tension.
pearls: Always size the Zitelli bilobed primary lobe at 100% of the defect diameter to prevent alar rim retraction, and undermine widely around the periphery to prevent trapdooring.
pitfalls: Designing a bilobed arc >110° creates severe standing cones and nasal asymmetry.

references.book: Zitelli JA. Arch Dermatol (The Bilobed Flap for Nasal Reconstruction)
